ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All participants gave informed consent, and procedures were approved by the institutional review board at the University of Michigan.

In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions.

Participants were recruited using Prolific's U.S. representative sampling option, which balances quotas for age, sex, and ethnicity to approximate U.S. census distributions (49.2% female, 48.7% male, 1.8% non-binary, 0.3% other or not reported; M age = 45.9, SD = 15.9, range = 19-85; 61.9% White, 12.6% Black, 6.4% Hispanic/Latino, 5.7% Asian, 11.3% multiracial, 2.1% other or not reported; 59.5% held a bachelor's degree or higher).
Participants were paid $12/hr for the 30-minute study, which ran on oTree, an open-source platform for online behavioral experiments (Chen et al., 2016).

table.text: Participants were instructed to portray either extraversion or introversion in a blog-style writing task.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions.

When writing their posts, extraversion-assigned participants were told to emphasize times they were outgoing, energetic, talkative, or socially engaged; introversion-assigned participants, times they were reflective, thoughtful, reserved, or preferred quiet activities.
In both conditions, participants were told that even if they did not usually see themselves this way, they should focus on moments when they did.

In the AI-Draft condition, each prompt was accompanied by a fully AI-generated text portraying the assigned trait and written in the first person; participants were instructed to revise the draft to reflect their own life and experiences while preserving the overall tone, with explicit guidance to adjust specific details rather than rewrite the paragraph entirely.

Following Gonzales and Hancock (2008), participants were told after the writing task that a "true" rating of their personality was needed for later analysis and rated themselves on 10 extraversion-related bipolar adjective pairs using 11-point scales.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A preregistered power analysis (G*Power; Faul et al., 2009) for a one-way ANOVA across the three authorship conditions (f = 0.25, α = .05, power = .95) required 252 participants.

The trait difference was 5.25 scale points in Manual, 6.35 in AI-Outline, and 6.89 in AI-Draft (Table S1), so the point estimates ran opposite to the predicted gradient. Within conditions, the trait difference was significant in AI-Outline, 95% CI [0.32, 12.39], p = .039, d = 0.37, and AI-Draft, 95% CI [0.10, 13.68], p = .047, d = 0.36, but not in Manual, 95% CI [-1.69, 12.18], p = .137, d = 0.26 (Table S1). Because each within-condition comparison had limited power (.43-.45 at d = 0.32), this pattern does not indicate that the effect differed by condition, consistent with the null Trait × Authorship interaction.

Participants were instructed to portray either extraversion or introversion in a blog-style writing task.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions.

When writing their posts, extraversion-assigned participants were told to emphasize times they were outgoing, energetic, talkative, or socially engaged; introversion-assigned participants, times they were reflective, thoughtful, reserved, or preferred quiet activities.
In both conditions, participants were told that even if they did not usually see themselves this way, they should focus on moments when they did.

In the AI-Draft condition, each prompt was accompanied by a fully AI-generated text portraying the assigned trait and written in the first person; participants were instructed to revise the draft to reflect their own life and experiences while preserving the overall tone, with explicit guidance to adjust specific details rather than rewrite the paragraph entirely.

Following Gonzales and Hancock (2008), participants were told after the writing task that a "true" rating of their personality was needed for later analysis and rated themselves on 10 extraversion-related bipolar adjective pairs using 11-point scales.

For fluency of self-presentation, participants completed eight items adapted from Shulman and Sweitzer (2018), following Ross and DeAndrea (2026) (e.g., "Overall, I found the task to be difficult," reverse-coded; M = 5.17, SD = 1.12, α = .88), with higher scores indicating a more fluent self-presentation.

text.text: Identity shift theory holds that selective online self-presentation can shift self-perception toward the portrayed identity, but its mechanisms assume that the presenter wrote the presentation.
Generative AI now lets people publish self-presentations they did not fully compose.

In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions.
AI involvement changed the writing process.

Participants in both AI conditions searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples, and participants who edited an AI draft felt less ownership of their text than those who wrote from an AI outline.
Neither process accounted for the shift.
The presenter need not be the sole author of a self-presentation for it to shape self-perception.
Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping how people present themselves online.
Selfpresentation, the strategic curation of behavior and messages to shape how others see us, is a social process with psychological consequences.
How people portray themselves feeds back into how they see themselves, especially when the portrayal is public (Bem, 1972; Goffman, 1959; Schlenker, 1985; Tice, 1992).

text.text: Identity shift theory (IST) extends this logic to computer-mediated communication, proposing that selectively presenting oneself online shifts self-perception toward the presented traits (Gonzales & Hancock, 2008).

text.text: IST was developed, however, in an era of human-authored communication, and its mechanisms presuppose that the person presenting the identity is also the person who wrote the presentation.
GenAI text-based writing tools (hereafter "AI," for brevity) remove that assumption, because a self-presentation may now be generated or revised by a system other than the self.
Unlike simpler text-editing or autocomplete features, AI can generate, refine, and rephrase text iteratively and in context-sensitive ways, which creates competing possibilities for IST.
On one hand, identity shift is thought to arise partly through processes engaged while composing the presentation.

When constructing a self-presentation, especially one they know is public, writers selectively retrieve memories consistent with the trait they are portraying (i.e., engage in biased scanning), attend to how they are describing themselves, and revise the text (Carr et al., 2021; Gonzales & Hancock, 2008).

The present study therefore tests whether the amount of authorship a person retains while composing a selective self-presentation affects subsequent identity shift.

Adapting prior designs (Gonzales & Hancock, 2008; Tice, 1992; Walther et al., 2011), we randomly assigned participants to present themselves as extraverted or introverted in one of three authorship conditions: Participants wrote the presentation themselves (Manual), wrote from an AI-generated outline (AI-Outline), or edited an AI-generated draft (AI-Draft).

text.text: Across this body of work, participants wrote the self-presentation themselves, so IST has never had to ask whether the person presenting the identity must also be its author for the effects to hold.
However, as communication technologies increasingly incorporate AI systems capable of producing self-presentational text, this assumption warrants and invites direct examination.
We suggest that the processes thought to drive internalization, such as investing effort in the wording and drawing on one's own experiences, are engaged in the act of composing.

The more of that composition a writer delegates to AI, the less these processes should be engaged, so we predict that identity shift will weaken as authorship moves from the self to the system: H1 (Authorship gradient): Post-task alignment with the assigned trait (i.e., identity shift) will be strongest in the Manual condition, intermediate in the AI-Outline condition, and weakest in the AI-Draft condition.
Online self-presentations may now range from fully self-written to fully AI-generated.
We focus on the composition stage, where authorship most directly intervenes, and hold constant the conditions outside it (e.g., feedback).

text.text: It develops through control, investment of effort, and intimate knowledge (Pierce et al., 2003; Van Dyne & Pierce, 2004), and a conventional self-presentation task engages all three.

text.text: When individuals compose a self-presentational message, they exercise control over what aspects of themselves they highlight, invest effort in selecting memories and crafting language, and develop intimate knowledge of the resulting text through revision and reflection.
From this perspective, the resulting self-presentational message can come to feel like an artifact that reflects and reinforces one's identity (Pierce et al., 2003).

text.text: If psychological ownership can be diminished in this way, the question for IST is whether internalization of the self-presentation (i.e., identity shift) still occurs.

For example, if a professional asks an AI tool to draft a LinkedIn bio that casts them as ambitious and driven, the bio that appears under their name may read as accurate, even flattering, while still feeling less like something they made and more like something they received.
We therefore treat authorship and psychological ownership as separate constructs in order to better understand how each contributes to identity shift.

A text experienced as "mine" can objectify and stabilize aspects of identity, inviting defense, justification, and incorporation into the self (Peck & Shu, 2009; Pierce et al., 2003), much as taking responsibility for a statement prompts people to adjust their private selfperceptions in order to maintain coherence (Festinger & Carlsmith, 1959; Schlenker et al., 1994; Tice, 1992).

text.text: By contrast, when a self-presentation is experienced as produced and owned by an external agent, discrepancies or shortcomings may be more readily attributed to the AI, reducing the need to reconcile or integrate the portrayal into the self-concept.

text.text: Classical accounts of biased scanning propose that when people are asked to portray a trait, they search memory for confirming experiences, which then serve as internal evidence that they possess the trait.

text.text: This is likely in part because classical accounts of the process describe it as largely automatic and thus not suitable for self-reported measures.

Therefore, we operationalize the component self-report can reach, which we call deliberate memory search, the effortful, motivated selection of trait-congruent memories and suppression of counter-trait ones during composition (e.g., "I deliberately searched for memories that showed me being [trait]").
AI authorship offers a natural test of this mechanism because it changes what the writer must do to produce the text.
When people compose a selective self-presentation themselves, the page is empty until they supply content, and retrieval of trait-consistent content from their own past is forced by the task.

In contrast, when AI supplies trait-congruent content, whether as an outline or as a full draft, writers may draw less on their own memories. Tice (1992) found that participants who drew on their own experiences to construct a self-presentation internalized the trait more strongly than those who delivered a presentation scripted by someone else.

text.text: That study differs from ours in three ways.
The presentation was delivered face to face rather than online, the script was written by another person rather than by AI, and participants delivered the script as written, without revising it.
Our AI-Outline and AI-Draft conditions fall between Tice's two poles, because participants received machine-generated content but still wrote or revised the text before publishing it.

If deliberate memory search drives internalization, the more content AI supplies, the less participants should search their memories, and the weaker the shift should be: H3 (Deliberate memory search mediation): Deliberate memory search will mediate the effect of authorship condition on post-task trait alignment (i.e., identity shift), such that lower authorship → reduced deliberate memory search → weaker identity shift.

text.text: Identification with a claim is distinct from the two mechanisms above.

Where ownership concerns whether the text feels like one's own, and deliberate memory search concerns how its evidence was gathered, identification concerns whether the portrayed identity fits the self.
Individuals may feel little ownership or engage in minimal deliberate memory search yet still judge a portrayal as a plausible or desirable self.
AI-mediated writing makes this fit especially consequential because AI readily generates coherent, trait-congruent portrayals.
For instance, suppose someone asks an AI tool to write their dating profile, and it returns one describing them as outgoing and spontaneous.
If they already see themselves as someone who could be that way, internalization may occur independent of composition.
If the presenter identifies with the content of the self-presentation, then endorsing and publishing it under their own name may be enough to produce shift regardless of who wrote the words.
If the profile describes someone they cannot imagine being, internalization may rely more heavily on drawing on past experiences and ownership that full authorship provides.

People low in identification should therefore be most exposed to the loss of authorship: H4 (Identification with a claim): Identification with the claim will moderate the authorship → identity shift relationship, such that the authorship gradient (H1) will be weaker when identification is high and stronger when identification is low.

text.text: All participants gave informed consent, and procedures were approved by the institutional review board at the University of Michigan.

Following prior identity shift experiments (Gonzales & Hancock, 2008; Tice, 1992; Walther et al., 2011), the study description told participants that the project examined psychology graduate students' ability to identify personality traits from online writing, and that their writing would be published on a public blog under their first name.

text.text: This cover story, standard in identity shift research, was implemented to lend credibility to the public-posting manipulation and mask the study's focus on self-perception so that post-task self-ratings would not reflect demand characteristics.

After consenting, participants completed demographics and the pre-task possible selfpresentation measure following Ross and DeAndrea (2026) and were then randomly assigned to one of six conditions by block randomization (blocks of six, one instance of each condition).

text.text: Participants then completed the writing task and the post-task survey.
Finally, they encountered a debriefing explaining that the public posting had been simulated and that their responses had not been shared outside the research team.
Participants were instructed to portray either extraversion or introversion in a blog-style writing task.
Assigning a trait allows identity shift to be detected as a between-group difference in post-task self-perception.
If presenting a trait shifts the self-concept, extraversion-assigned participants should later rate themselves as more extraverted than introversion-assigned participants.

Participants read a description of the assigned trait, completed an understanding check, and answered four open-ended questions about friends, family, hobbies, and school, and were instructed to draw from real past experiences consistent with the trait rather than fabricating responses.
Upon submission, participants saw a simulated blog page showing their post as a published entry under their first name, with the date and a visitor count.
Task instructions, outlines, drafts, and the publication screen are reproduced in the Supplemental Materials; Figure Note.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions.
Cell ns are analytic-sample sizes; 464 participants reached their assigned condition and 394 completed the study (see Supplemental Materials for attrition analyses).

When writing their posts, extraversion-assigned participants were told to emphasize times they were outgoing, energetic, talkative, or socially engaged; introversion-assigned participants, times they were reflective, thoughtful, reserved, or preferred quiet activities.
In both conditions, participants were told that even if they did not usually see themselves this way, they should focus on moments when they did.

The authorship manipulation formed a gradient of decreasing authorship, from full composition (Manual) to composition guided by AI-generated ideas (AI-Outline) to revision of AI-generated prose (AI-Draft).
In the Manual condition, participants wrote their responses entirely in their own words using a standard text-entry interface.

In the AI-Outline condition, each prompt was accompanied by three ChatGPT-generated bullet points framed as an outline to guide participants' thinking toward the assigned trait while they composed responses in their own words.

In the AI-Draft condition, each prompt was accompanied by a fully AI-generated text portraying the assigned trait and written in the first person; participants were instructed to revise the draft to reflect their own life and experiences while preserving the overall tone, with explicit guidance to adjust specific details rather than rewrite the paragraph entirely.

If participants attempted to submit without revisions or to delete the entirety of the text in the AI-Draft condition, they were given a reminder of the instructions to revise and the AI text was restored.
Each response required at least 50 words, with no time limit.

Because copy-and-paste was disabled in all conditions and attempted pastes were logged, participants could not import text from outside tools, including AI assistants, into their responses (see Behavioral Engagement).

All outlines and drafts were generated in advance with ChatGPT (GPT-4o, July 2025) using standardized prompts and were identical for all participants within a condition; they are reproduced in the Supplemental Materials.
Full item wording for all measures appears in the Supplemental Materials.
Post-task self-perceived extraversion was assessed with the bipolar adjective scales used in identity shift research (Fazio et al., 1981; Gonzales & Hancock, 2008; Walther et al., 2011).

text.text: After reverse-coding, ratings were summed to an extraversion score from 10 to 110 (M = 69.97, SD = 19.13, α = .88), with higher values reflecting a more extraverted self-perception.

The preregistered identity shift index rescales post-task extraversion so that higher values reflect self-perceptions more consistent with the assigned trait: the post-task score minus 60 for extraversion-assigned participants and 60 minus the post-task score for introversion-assigned participants (i.e., the signed deviation from the scale midpoint, oriented toward the assigned trait).

Orienting the index by assignment is essential because, as in prior work with this scale (Gonzales & Hancock, 2008; Ross & DeAndrea, 2026; Walther et al., 2011), introversionassigned participants scored above the midpoint in every condition (all Ms > 65); an unsigned distance from the midpoint would conflate trait-consistent and trait-inconsistent ratings in that group.

text.text: Psychological ownership was measured with five items adapted from Joshi and Vogel (2025) on 7-point scales (1 = strongly disagree,7 = strongly agree; the quality item,1 = very low,7 = very high; M = 5.84, SD = 1.07, α = .85).

One item asks about the quality of the post rather than ownership per se and correlated only .39 with the remaining four; we therefore report a four-item composite (α = .88; r = .98 with the five-item version) as a robustness check alongside the preregistered scale.
Higher scores reflect greater psychological ownership of the self-presentational content.

Four items developed for this study and preregistered measured deliberate memory search, the motivated selection of trait-congruent memories during composition (e.g., "I deliberately searched for memories that showed me being [trait]";1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree; M = 3.26, SD = 0.85, α = .70).
The items index the deliberate component of biased scanning (directed search, selective focus, suppression of counter-trait memories, strategic selection).

Five items, not preregistered, adapted from the accessibility subscale of the Memory Experiences Questionnaire (Sutin & Robins, 2007) asked how easily trait-relevant memories came to mind (e.g., "These memories were easy for me to recall"; 1-5; M = 4.09, SD = 0.73, α = .84), with negative items reverse-coded so that higher scores indicate easier retrieval.

text.text: Possible self-presentation was measured before random assignment, and fluency of self-presentation after the task.

For possible self-presentation, participants rated the stem "It is possible for me to present myself as..." for six adjectives from three of Fazio et al.'s (1981) bipolar pairs (extraverted/introverted, sociable/unsociable, talkative/quiet;1 = strongly disagree,7 = strongly agree); the three adjectives matching the participant's subsequently assigned trait were averaged into a matched composite (extraversion-assigned: M = 4.83, SD = 1.46, α = .86; introversion-assigned: M = 4.35, SD = 1.66, α = .88), with higher scores indicating that presenting the assigned trait felt more possible.

text.text: The two indicators capture identification with a claim at two stages, whether the assigned identity felt like a possible self before writing and whether it felt natural to enact afterward.

To assess behavioral engagement with the AI-generated text, editing intensity was operationalized as the normalized character-level Levenshtein distance between each participant's submitted text and the original AI-generated draft, expressing the proportion of the text that was modified (M = 48.0%, SD = 17.8%).

Because orientations toward AI could shape engagement with AI-assisted selfpresentations, we measured AI attitudes (M = 4.76, SD = 1.46, α = .92) and AI knowledge confidence (M = 5.12, SD = 1.06, α = .91) with items from Hong et al. (2021) on 7-point scales.

text.text: We return to the interpretation of the possible self-presentation result in the Discussion.
The central question of this study was whether identity shift requires full human authorship, or whether the effect persists when composition is partially delegated to AI.
Our findings show identity shift effects persist under AI-assisted writing.

Across all three authorship conditions, participants who portrayed extraversion subsequently rated themselves as more extraverted than those who portrayed introversion (d = 0.32), and the trait difference was of similar size in each condition and did not detectably differ across authorship conditions (ds = 0.26, 0.37, and 0.36; Table S1) (H1).

text.text: This held even though AI involvement changed how the presentation was produced.
Participants felt the text was less their own under AI drafting and searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples under AI assistance.
We take each finding in turn.

In previous identity shift studies, authorship and psychological ownership were fused in that participants wrote their own text, so the person presenting the identity was always the person who experienced the text as theirs.
The present experimental design decouples these constructs, because participants could present an identity in text they did not write, and indeed, our empirical results echo this dissociation.
Ownership was lowest when AI drafted the text.
AI-Draft participants reported less ownership than AI-Outline participants, and the difference from Manual participants was in the same direction but not significant.
This supports recent findings that AI involvement reduces felt ownership of self-relevant text (Draxler et al., 2024; Joshi & Vogel, 2025).

text.text: Yet identity shift did not differ across conditions, and ownership was unrelated to the shift on every test (path b p = .732; Ownership × Trait p = .908; Table S1).

text.text: Feeling that a self-presentation is one's own, in other words, is not a necessary condition for internalizing it.
At the same time, ownership responded to behavior.

Within the AI-Draft condition, participants who edited the AI-generated text more extensively reported greater ownership of it (r = .25, p = .005), consistent with the idea that people come to feel ownership of things they have invested effort in (Pierce et al., 2003).

text.text: Ownership rose with the amount of human contribution, then, but it was not what produced the shift.
One interpretation is that what internalizes a self-presentation is enacting and committing to it, rather than feeling ownership of its words.
A portrayal one revises, endorses, and publishes under one's own name may reshape self-perception even when the words were first written by someone, or in this case, something, else.
Two caveats apply.

First, ownership remained high in every condition (all Ms ≥ 5.6 on a 7point scale), plausibly because every condition required revision, which restores ownership of AI-assisted writing (Joshi & Vogel, 2025), so the data show that shift persists when ownership is reduced, not when it is low.

text.text: Second, the reduction was specific to drafting, since an AI outline left ownership intact.
One explanation is that psychological ownership tracks the words rather than the ideas.
A writer working from an outline still writes every sentence and so keeps the control, effort, and familiarity that build ownership (Pierce et al., 2003); a writer editing a draft does not.

text.text: This is consistent with evidence that ownership declines specifically as AI's share of the written text grows (Draxler et al., 2024; Joshi & Vogel, 2025), and it suggests ideational assistance and compositional assistance are not interchangeable inputs to felt ownership.

text.text: Ross and DeAndrea (2026) called for a return to biased scanning as the explanatory center of identity shift.
The present study provides a first self-report index of the deliberate component of that process, and the results do not support the classical account.
Neither link of the preregistered mediation ran in the predicted direction.

AI involvement increased deliberate memory search rather than reducing it, and more deliberate search predicted less identity shift, a significant negative indirect effect alongside a null total effect, or inconsistent mediation (MacKinnon et al., 2007).
text.formatted: AI involvement increased deliberate memory search rather than reducing it, and more deliberate search predicted less identity shift, a significant negative indirect effect alongside a null total effect, or inconsistent mediation <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(MacKinnon et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This negative association, however, mostly reflected participants' preexisting beliefs about the possibility of presenting as extraverted and introverted.
Once we controlled for how well each trait fit participants before the task, it shrank by 71% and fell to marginal significance, while the effect of authorship on search was unchanged.
Difficulty of retrieval (Schwarz et al., 1991) did not account for the pattern; memory accessibility did not differ by condition or moderate shift (r with deliberate search = -.10).
text.formatted: Difficulty of retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Schwarz et al., 1991)</ref> did not account for the pattern; memory accessibility did not differ by condition or moderate shift (r with deliberate search = -.10).

text.text: The safer conclusion is that deliberate search did not strengthen identity shift, not that it weakened it.
Items in the deliberate memory search measure probe whether participants searched for, focused on, and selected trait-consistent memories while setting aside inconsistent ones.

High scores therefore capture participants' awareness that they were curating their memories, which is likely strongest when the assigned trait fits a participant poorly, consistent with the measure's negative correlation with pre-task possible self-presentation (r = -.15).
This fits a discounting account.

Self-perception theory holds that people treat retrieved memories as evidence about themselves only when those memories feel like a fair sample (Bem, 1972; Fazio et al., 1981), and a writer who knows they went looking for confirming examples may experience them as examples they chose and assembled rather than as evidence of who they are.

text.text: On this reading, biased scanning is effective precisely when it is not deliberate.

The AI conditions turned writing into an explicit matching task ("here is a portrayal: find the parts of your life that fit it") and may have made participants aware of their selectivity without making the selected memories persuasive.
We offer this as a hypothesis for designs that manipulate awareness of selectivity directly.
Replicating Ross and DeAndrea (2026), pre-task possible self-presentation strongly moderated identity shift.
Participants who rated the assigned trait as more possible to present showed a larger gap in post-task self-ratings between trait conditions, the largest effect in the design (ΔR² = .313).
This is consistent with IST's identification-with-the-claim proposition (Carr et al., 2021) and with Ross and DeAndrea's conclusion that it is the theory's most robust moderator.
text.formatted: This is consistent with IST's identification-with-the-claim proposition <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Carr et al., 2021)</ref> and with Ross and DeAndrea's conclusion that it is the theory's most robust moderator.

text.text: Two caveats qualify this moderation, however.
The first concerns what the moderator actually measures.
The possible self-presentation items were designed to capture a belief: whether participants felt they could present themselves as extraverted or introverted.

Because we did not measure baseline personality, however, high scores may instead reflect personality itself -people who are extraverted will naturally report that presenting extraversion is possible for them.
Two patterns in the data are consistent with this reading.

Each pole correlated with posttask extraversion at .66 (possible extraversion) and -.63 (possible introversion), correlations as large as those typically found between two measures of the same trait, and nearly identical to the values Ross and DeAndrea (2026) report.

And when each pole was tested separately, neither moderated the trait effect (ps ≥ .54; Table S1), the pattern expected if the matched composite works by sorting participants on how extraverted they already are rather than by capturing identification with a claim.
text.formatted: And when each pole was tested separately, neither moderated the trait effect (ps ≥ .54; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>), the pattern expected if the matched composite works by sorting participants on how extraverted they already are rather than by capturing identification with a claim.

text.text: This concern applies only to the moderation.
Because trait portrayal was randomly assigned, the identity shift effect itself does not depend on how the moderator is interpreted.

Both readings, however, imply the same underlying condition: the assigned identity matched the participant's sense of self, whether as a belief about what they could enact, as their actual standing on the trait, or both.

That match is what the identification-with-the-claim proposition concerns, so we interpret matched possible self-presentation as an index of identity fit while remaining agnostic about its source. Ross and DeAndrea (2026) ground this proposition in personal standards from objective self-awareness theory, and our findings fit that framing as committing to an identity within one's personal standards promotes internalization, whereas committing to one outside them can reverse it, as in the boomerang effects observed at low identification (Ross & DeAndrea, 2026).

text.text: Separating the two accounts would require a baseline personality measure collected well before the task.
Read against IST's propositions (Carr et al., 2021), the findings reinforce some claims and raise new questions about others.

text.text: For the fundamental proposition, that selective selfpresentation produces identity shift, the results add a boundary specification.
The presenter need not be the sole author.

Enacting, personalizing, and publicly committing to a trait-consistent portrayal produced shift that did not detectably differ whether participants wrote from scratch, elaborated an AI outline, or edited an AI draft.
What remains untested is the case in which a person contributes nothing to the text, since every condition here involved compositional engagement.

A design in which participants publish AI-generated self-presentations unedited would establish whether it requires any compositional engagement and whether the self can be merely the endorser rather than the editor.

AI-assisted self-presentation is becoming routine in precisely the contexts identity shift theory describes: public, identity-relevant, and asynchronous portrayals such as dating profiles and professional materials.

Research on these contexts has long documented strategic enhancement, such as online daters embellishing identity characteristics (Ellison et al., 2006; Toma et al., 2008) and jobseekers inflating credentials (Guillory & Hancock, 2012), and has treated such embellishment primarily as a message aimed at an audience.

text.text: To the extent that AI tools generate enactable self-presentations at scale, users may come to see themselves in line with portrayals they did not fully compose.

Unlike online dating, where an eventual modality switch to face-to-face interaction supplies a corrective moment for idealized presentations (Ramirez & Zhang, 2007), many AI-assisted self-presentations have no equivalent point of disconfirmation.
text.formatted: Unlike online dating, where an eventual modality switch to face-to-face interaction supplies a corrective moment for idealized presentations <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ramirez & Zhang, 2007)</ref>, many AI-assisted self-presentations have no equivalent point of disconfirmation.

text.text: Moreover, our findings suggest the embellishment may not remain outwardfacing: AI-mediated self-presentations can shape how users see themselves, even when users recognize that the text is not entirely their own.

From a well-being perspective, this means that AI tools designed to help users craft positive, aspirational self-descriptions could facilitate beneficial identity exploration, such as trying on possible selves (Markus & Nurius, 1986) one could not have articulated independently.
text.formatted: From a well-being perspective, this means that AI tools designed to help users craft positive, aspirational self-descriptions could facilitate beneficial identity exploration, such as trying on possible selves <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Markus & Nurius, 1986)</ref> one could not have articulated independently.

text.text: On the other hand, the robustness of identity shift across authorship conditions raises the possibility that individuals could internalize self-presentations generated by AI systems optimizing for engagement or social desirability rather than authenticity, with implications for self-concept coherence over time.
Both possibilities warrant study in more naturalistic settings.
Several limitations qualify these findings.
The study used a single-session, simulated blog-posting task, whereas real-world self-presentation is repeated and more socially consequential.

The AI-generated content was produced by a single model and held constant within conditions; in practice it varies in quality, tone, and personalization; additionally, interactive generation, iterative prompting, or undesirable portrayals may moderate the effects observed here.

Finally, as noted previously, every condition required either writing or revision, so the design cannot determine whether any compositional involvement is necessary for identity shift; the unedited-publication design described above would provide that test.
A second set of limitations concerns measurement.

The deliberate memory search measure captures effortful, reportable search rather than the automatic retrieval classically theorized (Jones et al., 1981), and it was administered after the post-task self-rating, so it may partly reflect participants' inferences about their own process.

text.text: The design also omitted a baseline personality measure, following standard identity shift methodology (Gonzales & Hancock, 2008; Ross & DeAndrea, 2026; Walther et al., 2011), which avoids priming and self-consistency effects but prevents separating identification with the claim from trait standing.

text.text: Finally, completion was marginally lower under extraversion assignment and extraversion-assigned dropouts reported lower pre-task possible extraversion, so selective attrition could modestly inflate the overall trait difference; attrition did not differ by authorship condition, leaving the H1-H4 comparisons unaffected (Supplemental Materials).
The third limitation concerns what the null authorship effect can show.

The preregistered power analysis assumed a medium-sized authorship effect on the identity shift index, but any realistic attenuation of the d = 0.32 shift constitutes a small difference of differences, which requires a substantially larger sample to detect (Sommet et al., 2023); sensitivity and equivalence analyses in the Supplemental Materials converge on this point.

text.text: The null result therefore shows that we did not detect an authorship effect, not that none exists.
This study extends identity shift theory into the era of AI-mediated communication by asking whether the self must author a self-presentation for that presentation to reshape the self.

Within the bounds of this design, the answer is no: Identity shift replicated at an effect size comparable to prior work whether participants wrote from scratch, elaborated an AI-generated outline, or edited an AI-generated draft.

AI involvement changed how the presentation was produced, lowering felt ownership and increasing deliberate memory search, but neither process accounted for the shift, consistent with the possibility that the effects followed instead from enacting, personalizing, and publicly committing to the portrayal.
Whether AI weakens or amplifies the effect is a question for studies powered to detect a difference of differences.
As AI becomes a routine co-author of how people describe themselves, the self-presentations people publish may shape who they believe they are, regardless of who wrote the words.
